title: Rhythm, Sound & the Science of Music
objective: Students will understand the physics of sound — frequency, amplitude, and resonance — through the lens of jazz and blues instruments. They will connect the science of how instruments produce sound to why different instruments have distinct timbres, and explore how the human ear and brain process music.
materials: Device to play audio clips of individual instruments (trumpet, saxophone, double bass, piano, drums)
Rulers or string for simple wave demonstrations
Optional: tuning fork to demonstrate vibration

steps.title: What is sound?
script: Hold up a tuning fork (or tap a glass). Ask: *“What is sound, actually? What’s physically happening when you hear music?”* Take responses. Then play 10 seconds each of a trumpet, a bass, and a piano from the Jazz Lab — ask students what’s physically different between them.

screen.question: What is sound, actually? What’s physically happening when you hear music?

steps.purpose: Turn listening into a physics question.
students: Listen to each instrument for 10 seconds.

steps.title: Every sound is a wave
script: *“Every sound you hear is a wave — a vibration moving through air. High notes vibrate faster (high frequency). Low notes vibrate slower (low frequency). Loud sounds have bigger waves (high amplitude). Soft sounds have smaller waves. When Duke Ellington’s band played in Harlem in 1927, every instrument in that room was creating its own unique wave pattern — and your ears were doing the extraordinary work of separating them all out.”*

screen.caption: Every sound you hear is a wave — a vibration moving through air

steps.purpose: Name the two properties of a wave: frequency and amplitude.
students: Every sound you hear is a wave — a vibration moving through air.
Which is high frequency? Which is high amplitude?

steps.title: Timbre
script: *“The timbre — the unique color of each instrument — comes from its overtones. A trumpet playing middle C and a piano playing middle C produce the same fundamental frequency. But the trumpet has different overtone patterns from the piano, which is why they sound completely different. Jazz composers like Ellington understood this intuitively — he wrote specific parts for specific instruments because he knew exactly what wave patterns each one produced.”*

screen.text: The timbre — the unique color of each instrument — comes from its overtones.

steps.purpose: Explain why two instruments on the same note sound different.
students: Why do a trumpet and a piano playing middle C sound different?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Distribute student handouts. Students self-select their challenge level. Circulate with targeted questions to push thinking at each level.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Scaffolded activities with vocabulary support and structured response frames. Students engage with core content with guidance.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Independent grade-level analysis. Students apply concepts, make connections, and express their own thinking without heavy scaffolding.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Extended critical thinking and research. Students synthesize across sources, evaluate arguments, and produce original analysis or creative work.

steps.purpose: Apply the physics of sound to jazz instruments at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. You can switch at any time.

steps.title: Closing
script: Bring the class back together. Ask 2–3 students from different levels to share one thing they discovered or created. Close with:

*“The Harlem Renaissance wasn’t just a historical event. It was a demonstration that ordinary people — with talent, community, and courage — can create something that changes the world. The work you’ve done today connects you to that tradition.”*

screen.text: Ordinary people — with talent, community, and courage — can create something that changes the world.

steps.purpose: Share across the levels, and connect today’s work to the tradition.
students: Share one thing you discovered or created.
Exit ticket: *What is one connection between the Harlem Renaissance and Science?*
